text: Welcome to Data Visualization and Exploratory Data Analysis, the fourth course on the Data Scientist path. You already know how to wrangle data with pandas and summarize it with statistics. This course teaches the next skill: looking at data, and showing it to other people so they understand it and act on it.

In 1973, statistician Francis Anscombe published four tiny datasets, eleven points each, built so their summary numbers are nearly identical. All four share a mean x of nine, a mean y of seven point five, the same spread, and a correlation of zero point eight two. If you only read this table, you'd swear you had four copies of the same dataset.

Now draw them. Set one is a noisy but genuine straight line. Set two is a smooth curve; a straight line is the wrong model for it. Set three is a perfect line wrecked by one outlier pulling the fit upward. Set four has almost no relationship at all; a single extreme point manufactures the entire correlation.

Summary statistics compress a dataset into a few numbers, and compression throws away shape. A chart puts the shape back. That's the single best argument for why charts are not decoration; they're how you catch what a table cannot show.

Charts do two different jobs. Exploratory visualization is for you: quick, rough charts to find surprises and check assumptions, where polish doesn't matter. Explanatory visualization is for your audience: one message, the clearest chart for it, everything distracting removed. This course moves you from the first job to the second.

The road ahead: principles of visual communication, then matplotlib, seaborn and Plotly, then a systematic EDA workflow, then Power BI for data scientists, then communicating findings, ending in a capstone on a real dataset.
Always plot your data before you trust a summary of it. Next lesson: how to choose the right chart for the question you're actually asking.
